summary: Discusses the TCP mechanisms that cause trouble on links with high uncorrected error rates, and what can be done about them without adding intermediate devices. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: On a noisy phone line, here is how to keep talking without a middleman.

questions: why is tcp slow on wireless links
how does tcp tell congestion from packet corruption
subtitle: Why TCP slows down on links that corrupt packets, and which end-to-end mechanisms help without adding middleboxes.

tldr.problem: TCP treats every missing acknowledgement as a sign of congestion. On links with high uncorrected error rates, losses come from corruption instead, so TCP slows down far more than it needs to.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends implementing Fast Retransmit and Fast Recovery and Selective Acknowledgements (SACK), which repair losses quickly while keeping congestion avoidance intact, and it avoids any need for intermediate devices.
tldr.outcome: This is a Best Current Practice, not a new protocol: it says which existing TCP mechanisms to turn on, and which proposals (Delayed Duplicate Acknowledgements, Appropriate Byte Counting) it does not yet recommend.

facts.label: Window too small for fast retransmit

today: RFC 3155 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 50) published in August 2001, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its advice rests on the specifications of its time, such as [RFC2581], so read it as guidance from 2001.

sections.title: TCP Meets Unreliable Links
sections.content:
Congestion avoidance in the Internet assumes that most packet losses are caused by congestion. TCP's strategy treats the absence of an acknowledgement as a congestion signal. The RFC says this has worked well since it was introduced in 1988, because most links have low error rates.

Some links do not. The RFC names terrestrial and satellite wireless links. On them, a sending TCP can spend a long time waiting for acknowledgements that never arrive, and then send at much lower rates while it probes for a "safe" level, even though no buffer overflowed.

The goal is to improve use of available path capacity on such links without threatening Internet stability. The RFC assumes that major changes to the whole installed base of routers and hosts are not practical. It covers TCP only, not other transports such as UDP.
sections.eli5: TCP thinks every lost message means the road is too crowded, so it slows way down. On a bumpy road where messages get scrambled, that makes it crawl for no good reason.

sections.title: Is Your Link a High-Error Link?
sections.content:
All known subnetwork technologies have a non-zero bit error rate, and end stations cannot easily tell packets dropped by congestion from packets lost to transmission errors. The RFC offers a way to check, using the approximate TCP Reno response function from [PFTK98].

The formula gives the sending rate T from the packet size s, the round-trip time RTT, the retransmit timeout tRTO and the steady-state loss rate p. If the predicted rate is greater than the link speed, losses are not limiting TCP and the recommendations will not help. If it is lower, losses are limiting TCP.

Three caveats apply: use the end-to-end RTT rather than the link RTT; Max(1.0, 4*RTT) can stand in for tRTO; and bursty losses can make a loss rate measured over a long interval understate their effect.
sections.eli5: There is a math recipe that tells you whether your bumpy road really is slowing TCP down. If the answer is faster than the road allows, you do not have a problem.

sections.title: Why Not Use Proxies or Link-Layer Fixes?
sections.content:
The RFC covers end-to-end mechanisms that need no TCP awareness in intermediate nodes. That limits what endpoints can learn about losses, and attempts to guess the cause of a loss with heuristics have not been successful.

Performance Enhancing Proxies (PEPs, described in RFC 3135) can do better because they sit where network characteristics change. But the RFC calls generalized use of PEPs highly undesirable. The drawbacks it lists include loss of fate sharing, weaker end-to-end reliability and diagnostics, a block on network-layer security such as IPsec, harder mobility handoffs, trouble with asymmetric routing, more state to keep, and loss of QoS transparency. Not every PEP has every drawback, but the consequences must be weighed carefully.

The recommendations are for TCP over link layers that are already deployed. Designers who can still reduce errors at the link layer are the audience of a separate PILC document.
sections.eli5: You could put a helper in the middle of the road to fix problems, but a helper is one more thing that can break and can get in the way of secret messages. This RFC asks what the two ends can do on their own.

sections.title: Slow Start and Congestion Avoidance
sections.content:
Slow Start and Congestion Avoidance ([RFC2581]) are described as essential to the current stability of the Internet. High error rates make loss ambiguous, and TCP makes the "safe" choice of assuming congestion. Three out-of-order acknowledgements trigger fast retransmit and fast recovery. An expired retransmission timer triggers slow start.

Less reliable links often have small MTUs. Because the window grows in units of segments, a small MTU slows window growth during slow start. Path MTU discovery ([RFC1191]) must be used too, to prevent fragmentation, though several round trips may still be needed to open the window fully.

The recommendation here is simply that slow start and congestion avoidance remain, since they are MUSTs in STD 3 ([RFC1122]). Nothing in the document interferes with them.
sections.eli5: When TCP thinks the road is crowded, it starts again with tiny steps and speeds up gradually. That is a good safety rule, and this RFC keeps it.

sections.title: Fast Retransmit and Fast Recovery
sections.content:
A receiver that gets out-of-order data should send an acknowledgement immediately, repeating the next expected sequence number. These repeats are duplicate ACKs. When a sender sees three of them, fast retransmit lets it infer a loss and resend without waiting for the full retransmission timeout.

After a fast retransmit the sender halves its congestion window and uses fast recovery, running congestion avoidance from the halved window instead of restarting slow start from one segment. Because TCP uses additive increase and multiplicative decrease, a further loss before the window has recovered halves it again, which the RFC calls a downward spiral of the congestion window. If the error rate is constantly high, the window simply stays small.

A window smaller than four segments effectively prevents fast retransmit, and efficient recovery from several losses in one window needs NewReno ([RFC2582]). Short-lived connections, such as HTTP/1.0 closing a connection per resource, also keep windows small for reasons unrelated to errors.

Recommendation: implement Fast Retransmit and Fast Recovery. The RFC notes that [RFC2488] recommends them for satellite environments.
sections.eli5: If your friend keeps saying "I am still waiting for page 5," you resend page 5 right away instead of waiting a long time. But each time you do, you cut your speed in half, so lots of mistakes in a row make you very slow.

sections.title: Selective Acknowledgements
sections.content:
Selective Acknowledgements (SACK, [RFC2018]) let a sender repair several lost segments in one window without spending a round trip on each one. [RFC2883] adds a small extension that gives the sender more information about the order of delivery. In this RFC, SACK means the two together.

SACK is most useful in Long Fat Networks, where round-trip times are long and large windows raise the chance of several losses per window. It also helps where error rates are usually low but come in bursts: TCP grows its window between bursts, and SACK speeds recovery when a burst hits.

Recommendation: implement SACK as specified in [RFC2018] and updated by [RFC2883]. Where SACK cannot be enabled on both sides, senders may use NewReno to handle partial ACKs and multiple losses in a window.
sections.eli5: Instead of only saying "I am missing something," the receiver sends a list of exactly which pieces are missing, so the sender resends only those in one go.

sections.title: Summary and Open Topics
sections.content:
Since the Internet has no widely available way to tell congestion loss from transmission error, avoiding congestion has to take precedence over fast repair. The best achievable is to minimise time spent needlessly in congestion avoidance. The mechanisms are not limited to wireless environments.

For further work, the RFC points to Limited Transmit ([RFC3042]), which helps small windows that cannot produce three duplicate ACKs and which implementors should evaluate. It does not recommend Delayed Duplicate Acknowledgements, because no one knows how to compute the right delay for an arbitrary topology, nor Appropriate Byte Counting, which can increase burstiness when acknowledgements are lost. Explicit congestion notification cannot stand in for explicit transmission error notification.

At the application level, the RFC notes that HTTP/1.0 closes connections to mark the end of a resource, so TCP struggles to learn the path capacity. It calls proposals that share congestion information across connections, such as TCP Control Block Interdependence ([RFC2140]) and the Congestion Manager ([RFC3124]), critical to long-term stability.
sections.eli5: Turn on the two helpful tricks, keep the safety rules, and wait on a few other ideas until we know more about them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
As [RFC2581] points out, Fast Retransmit and Fast Recovery give an attacker a way to force connections to grind to a halt or, more dangerously, to behave more aggressively, which could lead to congestion collapse in some parts of the network. SACK is believed to neither strengthen nor weaken TCP's security properties.

Because the recommendations work end to end, they keep working under end-to-end IPsec, unlike PEPs implemented in intermediate nodes. There are no IANA considerations.
sections.eli5: A trickster could fake the "I am still waiting" messages to confuse TCP. Because the tricks only involve the two ends, secret-message wrappers like IPsec do not stop them from working.
